findings.source_passage: Had he been consulted, would he have cared to play the game at all, holding such cards as he held, and suspecting that the game was to be one of which neither he nor any one else back to the beginning of time knew the rules or the risks or the stakes?
findings.source_locator: second paragraph, after 'queer as to offer a subject of curious speculation'
findings.why_it_matters: This rhetorical question is one of the most critically cited passages in the chapter; it crystallizes Adams's governing game/chance metaphor and the theme of unearned fate vs. conscious agency. Its omission removes the intellectual machinery that makes the paragraph's conclusion ('consenting, contracting party') earn its meaning.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the full sequence: 'Had he been consulted, would he have cared to play the game at all…neither he nor any one else back to the beginning of time knew the rules or the risks or the stakes?' before arriving at 'He was not consulted and was not responsible.'

findings.source_passage: He was not consulted and was not responsible, but had he been taken into the confidence of his parents, he would certainly have told them to change nothing as far as concerned him. He would have been astounded by his own luck.
findings.source_locator: second paragraph, immediately after the 'rules or the risks or the stakes' sentence
findings.why_it_matters: This passage establishes the retrospective ironic self-assessment that is fundamental to Adams's autobiographical voice throughout the book; 'He would have been astounded by his own luck' is a signature Adams sentence widely quoted by critics.
findings.suggested_fix: Insert the full text from 'He was not consulted and was not responsible' through 'the more readily for knowing the exact values' before the 'consenting, contracting party' sentence.

findings.source_passage: No such accident had ever happened before in human experience. For him, alone, the old universe was thrown into the ash-heap and a new one created. He and his eighteenth-century, troglodytic Boston were suddenly cut apart—separated forever—in act if not in sentiment, by the opening of the Boston and Albany Railroad; the appearance of the first Cunard steamers in the bay; and the telegraphic messages which carried from Baltimore to Washington the news that Henry Clay and James K. Polk were nominated.
findings.source_locator: fourth paragraph, 'This problem of education, started in 1838…'
findings.why_it_matters: This is the central technological-rupture passage of the chapter and one of the most cited in the entire book; the three technologies (railroad, steamship, telegraph) are Adams's own catalogue of modernity's arrival and are interpretively indispensable for readings of his determinism and historical method.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the entire paragraph beginning 'This problem of education, started in 1838' including the specific trio of railroad/Cunard/telegraph and the date May 1844.

findings.source_passage: the boy looked out on the world with the instinct of resistance; for numberless generations his predecessors had viewed the world chiefly as a thing to be reformed, filled with evil forces to be abolished, and they saw no reason to suppose that they had wholly succeeded in the abolition; the duty was unchanged. That duty implied not only resistance to evil, but hatred of it. Boys naturally look on all force as an enemy… but the New Englander… had learned also to love the pleasure of hating; his joys were few.
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'The atmosphere of education in which he lived…'
findings.why_it_matters: The draft compresses to a single clause ('implied hatred of evil as well as resistance to it') losing the sustained ironic analysis of Puritan psychology—'love the pleasure of hating; his joys were few'—which is a voice-defining passage essential to Adams's social criticism.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'Boys naturally look on all force as an enemy…had learned also to love the pleasure of hating; his joys were few' as the conclusion of the resistance paragraph.

findings.source_passage: the man who pretended they were not, was in his eyes a schoolmaster—that is, a man employed to tell lies to little boys. Though Quincy was but two hours' walk from Beacon Hill, it belonged in a different world. For two hundred years, every Adams, from father to son, had lived within sight of State Street, and sometimes had lived in it, yet none had ever taken kindly to the town, or been taken kindly by it.
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'The bearing of the two seasons…'
findings.why_it_matters: The definition of a schoolmaster as 'a man employed to tell lies to little boys' is one of the most quoted satirical asides in Adams; combined with the Adams-vs-State-Street motif, this passage is interpretively indispensable to the chapter's argument.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the schoolmaster aphorism and the two-hundred-year Adams/State Street sentence in the seasons paragraph.

findings.source_passage: the seeds of a moral education would at that moment have fallen on the stoniest soil in Quincy, which is, as every one knows, the stoniest glacial and tidal drift known in any Puritan land.
findings.source_locator: paragraph about the school-walk episode, final sentence
findings.why_it_matters: This closing ironic flourish is the rhetorical payoff of the school-walk anecdote—Adams's characteristic geology-as-moral-metaphor—and critics regularly cite it as an example of his ironic register; its absence flattens the episode's conclusion.
findings.suggested_fix: Append the stoniest-soil sentence after 'For this forbearance he felt instinctive respect.'

findings.source_passage: Louisa was charming, like a Romney portrait, but among her many charms that of being a New England woman was not one. The defect was serious.
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'At that time, and long afterwards, the Consul's house…'
findings.why_it_matters: The Romney portrait simile and the dry 'The defect was serious' are hallmark Adams ironic compression; critics cite this as exemplary of his biographical prose style, and it characterizes Louisa Adams in a way the draft's summary entirely omits.
findings.suggested_fix: Insert 'Louisa was charming, like a Romney portrait, but among her many charms that of being a New England woman was not one. The defect was serious.' in the Madam section.

findings.source_passage: He never dreamed that from her might come some of those doubts and self-questionings, those hesitations, those rebellions against law and discipline, which marked more than one of her descendants; but he might even then have felt some vague instinctive suspicion that he was to inherit from her the seeds of the primal sin, the fall from grace, the curse of Abel, that he was not of pure New England stock, but half exotic.
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'Such a figure was even less fitted…'
findings.why_it_matters: The 'seeds of the primal sin, the fall from grace, the curse of Abel' formulation is a key interpretive passage for Adams's self-construction as a figure of mixed inheritance; the draft reduces it to 'doubts and rebellions' and 'quarter taint,' losing the theological-mythological register entirely.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the full sequence including 'the seeds of the primal sin, the fall from grace, the curse of Abel, that he was not of pure New England stock, but half exotic.'

summary: The draft omits or fatally compresses multiple high-priority signatures: the 'rules or risks or stakes' game passage, the technological rupture catalogue (railroad/Cunard/telegraph), and 'He would have been astounded by his own luck,' while also flattening several medium-weight voice passages including the schoolmaster definition, the stoniest-soil irony, the Romney portrait characterization of Louisa, and the 'seeds of the primal sin' formulation.
